claim: NatB substrates account for about 21% of the human proteome.
source: Its substrates account for about 21% of the human proteome, including well known proteins such as actin, tropomyosin, CDK2, and α-synuclein (αSyn).
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract without supporting data in the manuscript, but likely draws from established literature.

claim: NatB substrates include actin, tropomyosin, CDK2, and α-synuclein.
source: Its substrates account for about 21% of the human proteome, including well known proteins such as actin, tropomyosin, CDK2, and α-synuclein (αSyn).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about NatB substrates.

claim: Human NatB-mediated N-terminal acetylation of αSyn plays key roles in the pathogenesis of Parkinson's disease.
source: Human NatB (hNatB) mediated N-terminal acetylation of αSyn has been demonstrated to play key roles in the pathogenesis of Parkinson's disease and as a potential therapeutic target for hepatocellular carcinoma.
evidence: This claim is stated as established knowledge from prior studies.

claim: Human NatB is a potential therapeutic target for hepatocellular carcinoma.
source: Human NatB (hNatB) mediated N-terminal acetylation of αSyn has been demonstrated to play key roles in the pathogenesis of Parkinson's disease and as a potential therapeutic target for hepatocellular carcinoma.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from prior research.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of hNatB bound to a CoA-αSyn conjugate was determined.
source: Here we report the cryo-EM structure of hNatB bound to a CoA-αSyn conjugate, together with structure-guided analysis of mutational effects on catalysis.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by structural data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Structure-guided mutational analysis reveals functionally important differences between hNatB and human NatA.
source: This analysis reveals functionally important differences with human NatA and Candida albicans NatB, resolves key hNatB protein determinants for αSyn N-terminal acetylation, and identifies important residues for substrate-specific recognition and acetylation by NatB enzymes.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparisons and mutational data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Structure-guided mutational analysis reveals functionally important differences between hNatB and Candida albicans NatB.
source: This analysis reveals functionally important differences with human NatA and Candida albicans NatB, resolves key hNatB protein determinants for αSyn N-terminal acetylation, and identifies important residues for substrate-specific recognition and acetylation by NatB enzymes.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparisons and mutational data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Key hNatB protein determinants for αSyn N-terminal acetylation were resolved.
source: This analysis reveals functionally important differences with human NatA and Candida albicans NatB, resolves key hNatB protein determinants for αSyn N-terminal acetylation, and identifies important residues for substrate-specific recognition and acetylation by NatB enzymes.
evidence: This is supported by structural and mutational analysis data in the manuscript.

claim: Important residues for substrate-specific recognition and acetylation by NatB enzymes were identified.
source: This analysis reveals functionally important differences with human NatA and Candida albicans NatB, resolves key hNatB protein determinants for αSyn N-terminal acetylation, and identifies important residues for substrate-specific recognition and acetylation by NatB enzymes.
evidence: This is supported by mutational analysis and structural data presented in the manuscript.

claim: N-terminal acetylation predominantly occurs co-translationally on eukaryotic nascent chains emerging from the ribosome exit tunnel.
source: N-terminal acetylation (NTA) is an irreversible protein modification that predominantly occurs co-translationally on eukaryotic nascent chains emerging from the ribosome exit tunnel (Aksnes et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to support it.

claim: N-terminal acetylation occurs on ~80% of human proteins.
source: This modification occurs on ~80% of human proteins (Aksnes et al., 2016) and impacts several protein functions including complex formation (Scott et al., 2011; Monda et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2013; Arnaudo et al., 2013; Gao et al., 2016), protein localization (Behnia et al., 2004; Setty et al., 2004; Dikiy and Eliezer, 2014; Miotto et al., 2015; Forte et al., 2011), and the N-end rule for protein degradation (Hwang et al., 2010; Shemorry et al., 2013; Park et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: N-terminal acetylation impacts protein complex formation.
source: This modification occurs on ~80% of human proteins (Aksnes et al., 2016) and impacts several protein functions including complex formation (Scott et al., 2011; Monda et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2013; Arnaudo et al., 2013; Gao et al., 2016), protein localization (Behnia et al., 2004; Setty et al., 2004; Dikiy and Eliezer, 2014; Miotto et al., 2015; Forte et al., 2011), and the N-end rule for protein degradation (Hwang et al., 2010; Shemorry et al., 2013; Park et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with multiple citations.

claim: N-terminal acetylation impacts protein localization.
source: This modification occurs on ~80% of human proteins (Aksnes et al., 2016) and impacts several protein functions including complex formation (Scott et al., 2011; Monda et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2013; Arnaudo et al., 2013; Gao et al., 2016), protein localization (Behnia et al., 2004; Setty et al., 2004; Dikiy and Eliezer, 2014; Miotto et al., 2015; Forte et al., 2011), and the N-end rule for protein degradation (Hwang et al., 2010; Shemorry et al., 2013; Park et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with multiple citations.

claim: N-terminal acetylation impacts the N-end rule for protein degradation.
source: This modification occurs on ~80% of human proteins (Aksnes et al., 2016) and impacts several protein functions including complex formation (Scott et al., 2011; Monda et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2013; Arnaudo et al., 2013; Gao et al., 2016), protein localization (Behnia et al., 2004; Setty et al., 2004; Dikiy and Eliezer, 2014; Miotto et al., 2015; Forte et al., 2011), and the N-end rule for protein degradation (Hwang et al., 2010; Shemorry et al., 2013; Park et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with multiple citations.

claim: Seven NATs have been identified in humans to date: NatA, NatB, NatC, NatD, NatE, NatF, and NatH.
source: In humans, seven NATs have been identified to date: NatA, NatB, NatC, NatD, NatE, NatF, and NatH (Aksnes et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: NatA, NatB and NatC are responsible for the majority of NTA.
source: NatA, NatB and NatC are responsible for the majority of NTA (Starheim et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: NatA is a heterodimeric complex with a catalytic subunit NAA10 and an auxiliary subunit NAA15.
source: NatA and NatB are heterodimeric complexes, each with a distinctive catalytic subunit (NAA10 in NatA and NAA20 in NatB; Starheim et al., 2008) and a unique auxiliary subunit (NAA15 in NatA and NAA25 in NatB; Arnesen et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: NatB is a heterodimeric complex with a catalytic subunit NAA20 and an auxiliary subunit NAA25.
source: NatA and NatB are heterodimeric complexes, each with a distinctive catalytic subunit (NAA10 in NatA and NAA20 in NatB; Starheim et al., 2008) and a unique auxiliary subunit (NAA15 in NatA and NAA25 in NatB; Arnesen et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: NatC is a heterotrimeric complex that contains a catalytic subunit NAA30 and two auxiliary subunits NAA35 and NAA38.
source: NatC is a heterotrimeric complex that contains a catalytic subunit (NAA30) and two auxiliary subunits (NAA35 and NAA38; Starheim et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: The auxiliary subunit of NatA plays an important allosteric role in substrate binding specificity and catalysis.
source: Structural and biochemical studies of NatA reveal that the auxiliary subunit plays an important allosteric role in substrate binding specificity and catalysis (Liszczak et al., 2013) and also contributes to ribosome binding during translation (Magin et al., 2017; Knorr et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: The auxiliary subunit of NatA contributes to ribosome binding during translation.
source: Structural and biochemical studies of NatA reveal that the auxiliary subunit plays an important allosteric role in substrate binding specificity and catalysis (Liszczak et al., 2013) and also contributes to ribosome binding during translation (Magin et al., 2017; Knorr et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: NatA accounts for 38% of the human N-terminal acetylome.
source: NatA accounts for 38% of the human N-terminal acetylome, acetylating small N-terminal residues after removal of the initial methionine residue (Arnesen et al., 2009), while NatB modifies N-termini with sequences of MD-, ME-, MN-, and MQ- (Van Damme et al., 2012; Van Damme et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: NatA acetylates small N-terminal residues after removal of the initial methionine residue.
source: NatA accounts for 38% of the human N-terminal acetylome, acetylating small N-terminal residues after removal of the initial methionine residue (Arnesen et al., 2009), while NatB modifies N-termini with sequences of MD-, ME-, MN-, and MQ- (Van Damme et al., 2012; Van Damme et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: NatB modifies N-termini with sequences of MD-, ME-, MN-, and MQ-.
source: NatA accounts for 38% of the human N-terminal acetylome, acetylating small N-terminal residues after removal of the initial methionine residue (Arnesen et al., 2009), while NatB modifies N-termini with sequences of MD-, ME-, MN-, and MQ- (Van Damme et al., 2012; Van Damme et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: NatB is conserved from yeast to human in both complex composition and substrate specificity profile.
source: NatB is conserved from yeast to human in both complex composition and in its substrate specificity profile (Starheim et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: Deletion of NAA20 or NAA25 in Saccharomyces cerevisiae leads to slower growth rate, diminished mating, defects in actin cable formation, and aberrant mitochondrial and vacuolar inheritance.
source: Deletion of either NAA20 or NAA25 leads to similar phenotypes including slower growth rate, diminished mating, defects in actin cable formation, and aberrant mitochondrial and vacuolar inheritance (Polevoda et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: Disruption of hNatB by knockout leads to defects in proper actin cytoskeleton structure, cell cycle progression, and cell proliferation.
source: In humans, disruption of NatB (hNatB) by knockout leads to defects in proper actin cytoskeleton structure, cell cycle progression, and cell proliferation (Starheim et al., 2008; Ametzazurra et al., 2008; Ametzazurra et al., 2009; Neri et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: hNatB is upregulated in human hepatocellular carcinoma.
source: In addition, hNatB is upregulated in human hepatocellular carcinoma (Ametzazurra et al., 2008), where it has been suggested as a potential therapeutic target as silencing of this complex can block cell proliferation and tumor formation (Neri et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Silencing of hNatB can block cell proliferation and tumor formation in hepatocellular carcinoma.
source: In addition, hNatB is upregulated in human hepatocellular carcinoma (Ametzazurra et al., 2008), where it has been suggested as a potential therapeutic target as silencing of this complex can block cell proliferation and tumor formation (Neri et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: hNatB-mediated NTA of α-synuclein increases αSyn stability and lipid binding.
source: hNatB-mediated NTA of α-synuclein (αSyn) has been shown to increase αSyn stability and lipid binding, and to reduce aggregation capacity (Dikiy and Eliezer, 2014; Watson and Lee, 2019; Mason et al., 2016; Maltsev et al., 2012; Trexler and Rhoades, 2012; Fernández and Lucas, 2018; Fauvet et al., 2012; Kang et al., 2012; Iyer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with multiple citations.

claim: hNatB-mediated NTA of α-synuclein reduces aggregation capacity.
source: hNatB-mediated NTA of α-synuclein (αSyn) has been shown to increase αSyn stability and lipid binding, and to reduce aggregation capacity (Dikiy and Eliezer, 2014; Watson and Lee, 2019; Mason et al., 2016; Maltsev et al., 2012; Trexler and Rhoades, 2012; Fernández and Lucas, 2018; Fauvet et al., 2012; Kang et al., 2012; Iyer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with multiple citations.

claim: hNAA20 and hNAA25 share only ~40% and ~20% sequence identity with the Candida albicans homolog, respectively.
source: However, hNAA20 and hNAA25 share only ~40% and~20% sequence identity with the Candida albicans homolog (Hong et al., 2017), respectively.
evidence: This is stated as a fact with a citation.

claim: Recombinant hNatB complex with full-length hNAA25 and C-terminally truncated hNAA20 (residue 1–163 out of 178 total residues) can be expressed in baculovirus-infected Sf9 insect cells and purified to homogeneity.
source: While attempts to express recombinant hNatB in E. coli were unsuccessful, we found that overexpression of hNatB complex with full-length hNAA25 (residues 1–972) and C-terminally truncated hNAA20 (residue 1–163 out of 178 total residues) in baculovirus-infected Sf9 insect cells produced soluble protein that could be purified to homogeneity (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Attempts to express recombinant hNatB in E. coli were unsuccessful.
source: While attempts to express recombinant hNatB in E. coli were unsuccessful, we found that overexpression of hNatB complex with full-length hNAA25 (residues 1–972) and C-terminally truncated hNAA20 (residue 1–163 out of 178 total residues) in baculovirus-infected Sf9 insect cells produced soluble protein that could be purified to homogeneity (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: Purified recombinant hNatB is active against the 'MDVF' peptide substrate.
source: In agreement with in vivo studies (Van Damme et al., 2012; Anderson et al., 2006; Ohrfelt et al., 2011; Theillet et al., 2016), we observed that the purified recombinant hNatB was active against this 'MDVF' peptide, while no activity could be observed in the absence of either the enzyme or peptide (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: hNatB shows no observable activity if the first residue 'M' is removed from the αSyn peptide substrate.
source: hNatB also showed no observable activity if either the first residue 'M' or the first two residues 'MD' in this αSyn peptide substrate was removed ('DVFM' peptide sequence: NH2-DVFMKGLRWGRPVGRRRRP-COOH; 'VFMK' peptide sequence: NH2-VFMKGLSRWGRPVGRRRRP-COOH; Figure 1B), suggesting that peptide substrate recognition by NatB is highly dependent on the first two N-terminal residues.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: hNatB shows no observable activity if the first two residues 'MD' are removed from the αSyn peptide substrate.
source: hNatB also showed no observable activity if either the first residue 'M' or the first two residues 'MD' in this αSyn peptide substrate was removed ('DVFM' peptide sequence: NH2-DVFMKGLRWGRPVGRRRRP-COOH; 'VFMK' peptide sequence: NH2-VFMKGLSRWGRPVGRRRRP-COOH; Figure 1B), suggesting that peptide substrate recognition by NatB is highly dependent on the first two N-terminal residues.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Peptide substrate recognition by NatB is highly dependent on the first two N-terminal residues.
source: hNatB also showed no observable activity if either the first residue 'M' or the first two residues 'MD' in this αSyn peptide substrate was removed ('DVFM' peptide sequence: NH2-DVFMKGLRWGRPVGRRRRP-COOH; 'VFMK' peptide sequence: NH2-VFMKGLSRWGRPVGRRRRP-COOH; Figure 1B), suggesting that peptide substrate recognition by NatB is highly dependent on the first two N-terminal residues.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing loss of activity when the first two residues are removed.

claim: hNatB is only active toward its unique canonical substrate type, displaying no overlapping activity toward other NAT substrates.
source: Consistent with previous results (Van Damme et al., 2012), hNatB is only active toward its unique canonical substrate type, displaying no overlapping activity toward other NAT substrates.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding consistent with prior literature, supported by data in Figure 1B.

claim: The CoA-αSyn conjugate has an IC50 of about 1.63 ± 0.13 µM.
source: Half-maximum inhibitory concentration (IC50) determinations revealed that this CoA-αSyn conjugate had an IC50 of about 1.63 ± 0.13 µM (Figure 1C), significantly lower than the Km values we had determined for hNatB toward a 'MDVF' peptide (45.08 ± 3.15 µM) and acetyl-CoA (47.28 ± 5.70 µM) (Table 1).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The Km value of hNatB toward the 'MDVF' peptide is 45.08 ± 3.15 µM.
source: Half-maximum inhibitory concentration (IC50) determinations revealed that this CoA-αSyn conjugate had an IC50 of about 1.63 ± 0.13 µM (Figure 1C), significantly lower than the Km values we had determined for hNatB toward a 'MDVF' peptide (45.08 ± 3.15 µM) and acetyl-CoA (47.28 ± 5.70 µM) (Table 1).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: The Km value of hNatB toward acetyl-CoA is 47.28 ± 5.70 µM.
source: Half-maximum inhibitory concentration (IC50) determinations revealed that this CoA-αSyn conjugate had an IC50 of about 1.63 ± 0.13 µM (Figure 1C), significantly lower than the Km values we had determined for hNatB toward a 'MDVF' peptide (45.08 ± 3.15 µM) and acetyl-CoA (47.28 ± 5.70 µM) (Table 1).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: A 3.46 Å-resolution cryo-EM three-dimensional map of hNatB was determined from 982,420 particles.
source: A 3.46 Å-resolution cryo-EM three-dimensional (3D) map was determined from 982,420 particles, selected from 5281 raw electron micrographs (Table 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Table 2 and supplementary figures.

claim: The central core region of the EM map contains excellent sidechain density with a local resolution of ~2.5 Å.
source: The central core region of the EM map contains excellent sidechain density with a local resolution of ~2.5 Å, particularly around the catalytic subunit, hNAA20.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the cryo-EM data.

claim: The atomic model of hNatB features a catalytic subunit, hNAA20, that adopts a canonical Gcn5-related N-acetyltransferase (GNAT) fold.
source: Consistent with previous NAT structural studies, the atomic model of hNatB features a catalytic subunit, hNAA20, that adopts a canonical Gcn5-related N-acetyltransferase (GNAT) fold (Deng and Marmorstein, 2020; Neuwald and Landsman, 1997).
evidence: This is stated as a structural finding consistent with prior knowledge.

claim: The auxiliary subunit hNAA25 is composed of a total of 39 α-helices.
source: Additionally, the model reveals that the auxiliary subunit hNAA25 is composed of a total of 39 α-helices among where the predicted first and second α-helices were built as poly-alanine due to a lack of resolvable sidechain density (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a primary structural finding from the cryo-EM model.

claim: The 39 α-helices of hNAA25 can be divided into three groups: an N-terminal region (α1-α8), a core region (α9-α29), and a C-terminal region (α30-α39).
source: The 39 α-helices can be roughly divided into three groups: an N-terminal region: α1-α8; a core region: α9-α29; and a C-terminal region: α30-α39 (Figure 2A and Video 1).
evidence: This is a structural classification based on the cryo-EM model.

claim: The N-terminal region of hNAA25 displays relatively weak EM density compared to other regions, suggesting that it is relatively flexible.
source: The N-terminal region (residue 1–164) displays relatively weak EM density compared to other regions, suggesting that it is relatively flexible (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the EM density data.

claim: The eight helices of the N-terminal region of hNAA25 form four helical bundle tetratricopeptide repeat (TPR) motifs.
source: The eight helices of the N-terminal region form four helical bundle tetratricopeptide repeat (TPR) motifs, which often participate in protein-protein interactions.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the model.

claim: The N-terminal TPR motifs of hNAA25 may participate in ribosome association, similar to the N-terminal region of the NAA15 auxiliary subunits of Schizosaccharomyces pombe and Saccharomyces cerevisiae NatA.
source: While there are no visible contacts between the N-terminal TPR motifs and hNAA20, it is possible that this region participates in ribosome association, similar to the N-terminal region of the NAA15 auxiliary subunits of Schizosaccharomyces pombe (Magin et al., 2017) and Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Knorr et al., 2019) NatA.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on structural similarity and prior knowledge.

claim: The 21 helices of the core region of hNAA25 form a number of TPR motifs, which come together to form a ring that completely wraps around and extensively contacts hNAA20 within its hollow center.
source: The 21 helices of the core region also form a number of TPR motifs, which come together to form a ring that completely wraps around and extensively contacts hNAA20 within its hollow center (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM model.

claim: The interaction between hNAA20 and the TPR motifs of the core region of hNAA25 buries a total interface area of about 2300 Å2.
source: Indeed, the interaction between hNAA20 and the TPR motifs of this core region buries a total interface area of about 2300 Å2.
evidence: This is a quantitative structural analysis from the model.

claim: The α28 helix of hNAA25 closes the core ring structure, locking hNAA20 in position, and bridging the N- and C-terminal regions.
source: The α28 helix closes the core ring structure, locking hNAA20 in position, and bridging the N- and C-terminal and regions.
evidence: This is a structural observation and functional inference from the model.

claim: The C-terminal region of hNAA25 features helices that bundle together to protrude out of the plane of the core ring structure at an angle of ~45°.
source: The C-terminal region features helices that bundle together to protrude out of the plane of the core ring structure at an angle of ~45° (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM model.

claim: The sequence identity of the catalytic subunits of hNatA and hNatB is 20%.
source: The sequence identity of the catalytic and auxiliary subunits of hNatA and hNatB are 20% and 15%, respectively.
evidence: This is stated as a fact from sequence comparison.

claim: The sequence identity of the auxiliary subunits of hNatA and hNatB is 15%.
source: The sequence identity of the catalytic and auxiliary subunits of hNatA and hNatB are 20% and 15%, respectively.
evidence: This is stated as a fact from sequence comparison.

claim: Between the catalytic subunits of hNatA and hNatB, there is a high degree of superposition (1.151 Å root-mean-square deviation over 105 common Cα atoms).
source: Between the catalytic subunits, there is a high degree of superposition (1.151 Å root-mean-square deviation [RMSD] over 105 common Cα atoms), except for an additional helix, α5, on the C-terminus of hNatA-NAA10, which is absent in hNatB-NAA20 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a quantitative structural comparison.

claim: hNatA-NAA10 has an additional helix, α5, on the C-terminus, which is absent in hNatB-NAA20.
source: Between the catalytic subunits, there is a high degree of superposition (1.151 Å root-mean-square deviation [RMSD] over 105 common Cα atoms), except for an additional helix, α5, on the C-terminus of hNatA-NAA10, which is absent in hNatB-NAA20 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the comparison.

claim: The core regions of hNatA-NAA15 and hNatB-NAA25 display similar topology with an RMSD of 8.369 Å over 262 common Cα atoms.
source: Between the auxiliary subunits, the core and N-terminal regions of both hNatA-NAA15 and hNatB-NAA25 display similar topology, although a higher degree of deviation than the catalytic subunits. The core regions both wrap around their respective catalytic subunits (8.369 Å RMSD over 262 common Cα atoms), while the N-terminal regions jut off to the side (7.360 Å RMSD over 55 common Cα atoms).
evidence: This is a quantitative structural comparison.

claim: The N-terminal regions of hNatA-NAA15 and hNatB-NAA25 have an RMSD of 7.360 Å over 55 common Cα atoms.
source: Between the auxiliary subunits, the core and N-terminal regions of both hNatA-NAA15 and hNatB-NAA25 display similar topology, although a higher degree of deviation than the catalytic subunits. The core regions both wrap around their respective catalytic subunits (8.369 Å RMSD over 262 common Cα atoms), while the N-terminal regions jut off to the side (7.360 Å RMSD over 55 common Cα atoms).
evidence: This is a quantitative structural comparison.

claim: The C-terminal regions of hNatA-NAA15 and hNatB-NAA25 diverge significantly from one another.
source: By contrast, the C-terminal regions of hNatA-NAA15 and hNatB-NAA25 diverge significantly from one another.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the comparison.

claim: The C-terminal region of hNAA25 is oriented toward its N-terminal region.
source: For hNA25, the C-terminal region of hNAA25 is oriented toward its N-terminal region, while the C-terminal region of hNAA15 is positioned ~50 Å away from the relative position of the superimposed C-terminal domain of hNAA25 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the model.

claim: The C-terminal region of hNAA15 is positioned ~50 Å away from the relative position of the superimposed C-terminal domain of hNAA25.
source: For hNA25, the C-terminal region of hNAA25 is oriented toward its N-terminal region, while the C-terminal region of hNAA15 is positioned ~50 Å away from the relative position of the superimposed C-terminal domain of hNAA25 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a quantitative structural observation from the comparison.

claim: The positioning of hNAA25 may serve to promote hNAA25 intra-termini communication.
source: The positioning of hNAA25 may serve to promote hNAA25 intra-termini communication, which is similar to the interaction of hNatA and its regulatory protein HYPK (Gottlieb and Marmorstein, 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on structural observations.

claim: IP6 acts as 'glue' between the C-terminal and core domains in hNAA15 and hNAA10 via a series of hydrogen bonds and electrostatic interactions.
source: Recent reports have described the role of the small molecule IP6 (inositol hexakisphosphate) in hNatA activity, where it is found to act as 'glue' between the C-terminal and core domains in hNAA15 and hNAA10 via a series of hydrogen bonds and electrostatic interactions (Gottlieb and Marmorstein, 2018; Cheng et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: An extended loop connecting the α31 helix with the α32 helix of hNatB-NAA25 mediates hydrophobic interactions between hNatB-NAA25 and -NAA20, likely serving a similar role as IP6 in hNatA.
source: While no corresponding small molecules have been identified to play a similar role in hNatB, our model shows that this interaction is replaced by an extended loop that connects the α31 helix with the α32 helix of hNatB-NAA25. This loop, which is not present in hNatA-NAA15, appears to mediate hydrophobic interactions between hNatB-NAA25 and -NAA20, likely to serve a similar role as IP6 (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is a structural observation and functional inference from the model.

claim: The superimposed structures of human and Candida albicans NatB revealed a high degree of structural conservation (NAA20: 0.698 Å RMSD over 125 common Cα atoms; NAA25 Core region: 3.267 Å RMSD over 266 common Cα atoms).
source: We also compared the structures from human and the previously described C. albicans NatB (CaNatB, PDB: 5K18). Although the two superimposed structures revealed a high degree of structural conservation (NAA20: 0.698 Å RMSD over 125 common Cα atoms; NAA25 Core region: 3.267 Å RMSD over 266 common Cα atoms), the N-terminal region of hNatB-NAA25 appears to overlay more closely to hNatA-NAA15 than to CaNatB-NAA25 (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is a quantitative structural comparison.

claim: The N-terminal region of hNatB-NAA25 appears to overlay more closely to hNatA-NAA15 than to CaNatB-NAA25.
source: We also compared the structures from human and the previously described C. albicans NatB (CaNatB, PDB: 5K18). Although the two superimposed structures revealed a high degree of structural conservation (NAA20: 0.698 Å RMSD over 125 common Cα atoms; NAA25 Core region: 3.267 Å RMSD over 266 common Cα atoms), the N-terminal region of hNatB-NAA25 appears to overlay more closely to hNatA-NAA15 than to CaNatB-NAA25 (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the comparison.

claim: The N-terminal regions of hNatB-NAA25 and hNatA-NAA15 are positioned more closely to the peptide substrate binding sites of the respective catalytic subunits compared to CaNAA25.
source: Compared to CaNAA25, the N-terminal regions of hNatB-NAA25 and hNatA-NAA15 are positioned more closely to the peptide substrate binding sites of the respective catalytic subunits.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the comparison.

claim: The relative shift in the position of the N-terminal regions of the human NAT auxiliary subunits, hNAA15 and hNAA25, may reflect a difference in the mechanism for ribosome association and co-translational NTA in C. albicans compared with humans.
source: Based on the role that the N-terminal yeast NatA-Naa15p regions play in ribosome docking (Magin et al., 2017; Knorr et al., 2019), we propose that the relative shift in the position of the N-terminal regions of the human NAT auxiliary subunits, hNAA15 and hNAA25, may reflect a difference in the mechanism for ribosome association and co-translational NTA in C. albicans compared with humans.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on structural observations and prior knowledge.

claim: CoA enters the catalytic active site through a groove formed by α3 and α4 of the catalytic subunit.

evidence: This is a structural observation consistent with other NATs.

claim: The peptide substrate enters the active site on the opposite side of the catalytic subunit flanked by the α1–2 and β6-β7 loops.

claim: R84A, R85A, and G87A mutants did not show significant defects in overall protein catalytic function.
source: Among them, R84A, R85A, and G87A did not show significant defects in overall protein catalytic function (Table 1).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Table 1.

claim: Y123A mutant nearly abolished protein activity, with a 95% loss of protein activity, affecting both kcat and Km.
source: However, a Y123A mutant nearly abolished protein activity, with a 95% loss of protein activity, affecting both kcat and Km (Table 1).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Table 1.

source: We observed that Y123F displayed a similar ~88% loss of kcat, but had a negligible effect on the peptide Km (Table 1).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Table 1.

claim: The Tyr123 hydroxyl group is critical for catalysis but not required for substrate binding.
source: These data suggested that the Tyr123 hydroxyl group is critical for catalysis but not required for substrate binding, while the aromatic ring of Tyr123 plays a role in peptide substrate binding.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutational data comparing Y123A and Y123F.

claim: The aromatic ring of Tyr123 plays a role in peptide substrate binding.
source: These data suggested that the Tyr123 hydroxyl group is critical for catalysis but not required for substrate binding, while the aromatic ring of Tyr123 plays a role in peptide substrate binding.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutational data comparing Y123A and Y123F.

claim: The hydroxyl group of Tyr123 is about 3.5 Å from the sulfur atom of the CoA-αSyn conjugate and 6.3 Å away from the αSyn N-terminus.
source: Given that the hydroxyl group of Tyr123 is about 3.5 Å from the sulfur atom of the CoA-αSyn conjugate and 6.3 Å away from the αSyn N-terminus, it is in a position to play a role as a general base or acid for catalysis, potentially through an intervening water molecule (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a quantitative structural observation from the model.

claim: Tyr123 is in a position to play a role as a general base or acid for catalysis, potentially through an intervening water molecule.
source: Given that the hydroxyl group of Tyr123 is about 3.5 Å from the sulfur atom of the CoA-αSyn conjugate and 6.3 Å away from the αSyn N-terminus, it is in a position to play a role as a general base or acid for catalysis, potentially through an intervening water molecule (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on structural observations and mutational data.

claim: Y27A mutation showed ~twofold higher Km.
source: We were surprised to find that mutations of hNatB residues that mediated backbone hydrogen bond interactions, Y27A and Y138A, had relatively modest effects on αSyn peptide NTA with Y27A showing ~twofold higher Km and Y138A showing ~twofold reduced Kcat, together suggesting that sidechain contacts might dominate the binding energy (Table 1).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Table 1.

claim: Y138A mutation showed ~twofold reduced Kcat.
source: We were surprised to find that mutations of hNatB residues that mediated backbone hydrogen bond interactions, Y27A and Y138A, had relatively modest effects on αSyn peptide NTA with Y27A showing ~twofold higher Km and Y138A showing ~twofold reduced Kcat, together suggesting that sidechain contacts might dominate the binding energy (Table 1).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Table 1.

claim: Sidechain contacts might dominate the binding energy for αSyn peptide NTA by hNatB.
source: We were surprised to find that mutations of hNatB residues that mediated backbone hydrogen bond interactions, Y27A and Y138A, had relatively modest effects on αSyn peptide NTA with Y27A showing ~twofold higher Km and Y138A showing ~twofold reduced Kcat, together suggesting that sidechain contacts might dominate the binding energy (Table 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the mutational data.

claim: H73A mutation produced a ~90% reduction in activity.
source: Consistent with this, and our structural observations, we found that H73A produced a ~90% reduction in activity (Table 1).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Table 1.

claim: hNAA20-His73 appears to play a critical role in cognate substrate recognition by hNatB.
source: This correlates with the importance of the His73 hydrogen bond and van der Waals contacts with αSyn-Asp2. Of note, other cognate hNatB sidechain residues at position 2, Glu, Gln, and Asn would also be well positioned to form hydrogen bonds with His73. Together, hNAA20-His73 appears to play a critical role in cognate substrate recognition by hNatB.
evidence: This is inferred from structural observations and mutational data.

claim: N116A mutant leads to ~90% loss in activity.
source: To test this, we prepared and evaluated an N116A mutant and, consistent with our hypothesis, Ans116, we found that this mutant leads to ~90% loss in activity (Table 1).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Table 1.

claim: hNatB-NAA20 residues His73, Asn116, and Tyr123 are functionally important in hNatB-mediated N-terminal acetylation.
source: Taken together, our structural and mutational analysis of hNatB highlight the functional importance of hNatB-NAA20 residues His73, Asn116, and Tyr123 in hNatB-mediated N-terminal acetylation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on structural and mutational data.

claim: Tyr123 appears to play a critical catalytic role, potentially as a general base and/or acid for catalysis.
source: While Tyr123 appears to play a critical catalytic role, potentially as a general base and/or acid for catalysis; His73 appears to play an important role in the recognition of substrate residue two and Asn116 likely plays a structural role (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is inferred from structural observations and mutational data.

claim: His73 appears to play an important role in the recognition of substrate residue two.
source: While Tyr123 appears to play a critical catalytic role, potentially as a general base and/or acid for catalysis; His73 appears to play an important role in the recognition of substrate residue two and Asn116 likely plays a structural role (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is inferred from structural observations and mutational data.

claim: Asn116 likely plays a structural role.
source: While Tyr123 appears to play a critical catalytic role, potentially as a general base and/or acid for catalysis; His73 appears to play an important role in the recognition of substrate residue two and Asn116 likely plays a structural role (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is inferred from structural observations and mutational data.

claim: His73, Asn116, and Tyr123 could employ a bridging water molecule to mediate their functional roles.
source: Each of these residues could employ a bridging water molecule to mediate their functional roles, although these putative water molecules are not visible at the current resolution of our structure.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on structural observations.

claim: hNatB can acetylate an α-Syn peptide in vitro.
source: We demonstrated for the first time that hNatB can acetylate an α-Syn peptide in vitro, directly linking hNatB to NTA of α-Syn.
evidence: This is stated as a primary finding of the study.

claim: αSyn-Met1 sits in a hydrophobic pocket that comfortably accommodates a methionine residue.
source: αSyn-Met1 sits in a hydrophobic pocket that comfortably accommodates a methionine residue, whereas shorter sidechains or longer polar or charged sidechains would fit poorly (Figure 5B–C).
evidence: This is a structural observation and inference from the model.

claim: Shorter sidechains or longer polar or charged sidechains would fit poorly in the Met1 binding pocket of hNAA20.
source: αSyn-Met1 sits in a hydrophobic pocket that comfortably accommodates a methionine residue, whereas shorter sidechains or longer polar or charged sidechains would fit poorly (Figure 5B–C).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations.

claim: The nature of the Met1 binding pocket in hNAA20 is similar to the described hNAA50 recognition of Met1.
source: The nature of this binding pocket is similar to the described hNAA50 recognition of Met1 (Liszczak et al., 2011; Figure 5B–C).
evidence: This is stated as a comparison with prior structural knowledge.

claim: The hNatB substrate client profile featuring D-, E-, N-, or Q-residues in position two is consistent with the mechanisms of substrate recognition observed in the binding pocket for αSyn-Asp2.
source: The hNatB substrate client profile featuring D-, E-, N-, or Q-residues in position two is consistent with the mechanisms of substrate recognition observed in the binding pocket for αSyn-Asp2.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations.

evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations.

claim: The second residue of hNatB substrates would form a hydrogen bond interaction with His73 and Thr75, which may accommodate the carboxyl sidechains of both the shorter D- and N- and longer E- and Q- sidechains.
source: This second residue would also form a hydrogen bond interaction with His73 and Thr75, which may accommodate the carboxyl sidechains of both the shorter D- and N- and longer E- and Q- sidechains.

claim: His73 and Thr75 are strictly conserved from yeast to man.
source: Notably, His73 and Thr75 are strictly conserved from yeast to man (Figure 5 and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from sequence analysis.

claim: Shorter polar or nonpolar sidechains would less efficiently fill the pocket for residue two in hNatB substrates.
source: In contrast, shorter polar or nonpolar sidechains would less efficiently fill the pocket for residue two, while larger polar or charged sidechains would likely result in steric clashes.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations.

claim: Larger polar or charged sidechains would likely result in steric clashes in the pocket for residue two in hNatB substrates.
source: In contrast, shorter polar or nonpolar sidechains would less efficiently fill the pocket for residue two, while larger polar or charged sidechains would likely result in steric clashes.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations.

claim: Mutation of hNAA50-Tyr31 (corresponding to hNaa20 residue Tyr27) had minimal effects on hNatB kinetic parameters.
source: While previous studies have suggested that hNAA50-Tyr31 plays an important role in catalysis, mutation of the corresponding hNaa20 residue, Tyr27, had minimal effects on hNatB kinetic parameters.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding.

claim: hNAA50 contains a tyrosine residue at the same position as hNAA20-Tyr123 (hNAA50-Tyr124).
source: Interestingly, hNAA50 contains a tyrosine residue at the same position (hNAA50-Tyr124), although the mechanistic significance of this tyrosine residue has not yet been described (Liszczak et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with a citation.

claim: hNatB is highlighted as a therapeutic target for αSyn toxicity.
source: Indeed, a recent study highlights hNatB as a therapeutic target for αSyn toxicity (Vinueza-Gavilanes et al., 2020).

claim: The structural information provided could aid in the rational development of more drug-like hNatB inhibitors with possible therapeutic applications.
source: Our development of a CoA-αSyn conjugate bisubstrate with an IC50 of ~1.6 µM represents a step in this direction, although the structural information provided here could further aid to the rational development of more drug-like hNatB inhibitors with possible therapeutic applications.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications of the findings.
